Charter contracts: the fee is fixed, the cost is yours

September 12, 2026 · By the Tailwinds team

There is a new Charters page under Company. Brokers post fixed-fee flying jobs — a tour operator’s weekly programme, a relief rotation into an awkward field, outsize freight that will not wait, a rival short of lift who needs a wet lease. You pick which ones to take, and which of your aeroplanes flies them.

The thing to understand before you sign anything: the cheque is the same whoever flies it. Every contract is priced against the cheapest current aircraft that could legally do the job. Send something thirstier and the difference comes out of your pocket. A 160-seat rotation out of San Francisco is priced as a 737 job; fly it with a 787 and you will lose money on a contract that looked generous on the board.

  • Where the work starts matters as much as where it goes. A contract out of an airport you already serve is nearly free to begin. One out of a city you have never flown to costs you two empty legs to position the aeroplane — fuel, crew and a week of block hours for no revenue — plus ground handling every week at a station where you have no staff and no contract rates. You do not need a gate at the far end, but you do pay for the privilege.
  • Some contracts are not worth taking, and they do not look any different. Roughly a quarter of the board is priced below what a competent operator can fly it for. There is no badge, no warning and no recommendation. Pick an aeroplane and the page shows you exactly what that aeroplane costs to fly the mission — fuel, crew, landing fees, handling, positioning, and the hours it eats. What it will not tell you is whether to sign. That is the game.
  • A wet lease hands the fuel bill to the customer. On an ACMI contract you supply the aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance, and they buy the fuel. Thinner margins than flying it yourself — and the right answer when fuel is spiking, which is exactly when more of it appears on the board.
  • Signing is a commitment. If the assigned aeroplane is in the shop when the week runs and nothing can take its place, you have breached the contract: you pay a penalty, and your reputation and your charter record both take it. A same-type reserve stationed at either end of the contract will step in and save it, which is the best reason yet to keep one standing by.
  • The board is earned. Brokers post work to carriers they have heard of. A brand-new airline sees two thin offers; one with real awareness, a solid reputation and a record of delivering sees a full board, better paid. Break a contract and that goes into reverse.
  • It follows the season and the world. Ski programmes in winter, Mediterranean series in summer, sub-service cover when a disruption is running, and a thinner board with tighter fees in a downturn.

A contract or two is a good way to earn from an aeroplane with spare hours, or to fly through the months your leisure routes are dormant. A schedule you run well still beats charter work per hour in the air, so this is a complement to your network rather than a replacement for it — the arithmetic behind that is in route economics, matching the right metal to the job is in the aircraft guide, and what your block-hour budget will actually take is in fleet planning.
